stem: Write the recurring decimal ${=n}.\overline{{=p}}$ as a single fraction in simplest form (not a mixed number). The bar marks the two digits that repeat for ever.
solution: Write the decimal out as an equation: $x = {=n}.{=rep}\ldots$
Two digits repeat, so multiply both sides by $100$. This moves the decimal point two places to the right and keeps the same recurring digits after it: $100x = {=big}.{=rep}\ldots$
Subtract the first equation from the second so that the recurring digits cancel: $100x - x = ({=big}.{=rep}\ldots) - ({=n}.{=rep}\ldots)$, which gives $99x = {=top}$.
Simplify: the highest common factor of ${=top}$ and $99$ is ${=g}$, so in simplest form $x = \frac{{=ans_n}}{{=ans_d}}$.
notes: The book's typical exercise: whole-number part plus a two-digit recurring block under a bar (12d 5.31 recurring, 12e and 12f 4.93 / 3.93 recurring, 11-6c 4.14 recurring). One multiplication (by 100), 99x = 99n + p. Blocks that are multiples of 11 (11, 22, ... 99) are excluded because they are really a single repeating digit and would be a different skeleton. Because gcd(99n + p, 99) = gcd(p, 99), about a third of instances reduce (to over 33 or over 11) and the rest stay over 99, mirroring the book's mix of 526/99 and 163/33; the last step is worded ('the highest common factor ... is g, so in simplest form') so it is true whether g is 1 or more. Stem asks for an improper fraction, as the book prints (526/99, 163/33). 729 instances; all checked by script (fraction equals the decimal to 50 places). Note on the book: its solution to 12b (0.6 then 3 recurring) prints '99x = 57' where the working gives 90x = 57; the final 57/90 is right, and this family does not copy that slip (it is not used here).
